title: Italian expansion (1933–1940)
summary: Mussolini's aims abroad, the invasion of Abyssinia and the League's failure, and Italy's drift from the Stresa Front into alliance with Hitler.

keyterms.definition: 'Our sea': Mussolini's aim to make the Mediterranean an Italian-dominated sea, echoing the Roman Empire.
April 1935 agreement of Britain, France and Italy to oppose German breaches of Versailles and protect Austrian independence.
December 1934 clash between Italian and Ethiopian troops at an oasis near the Italian Somaliland border, used as a pretext for war.
December 1935 secret British–French plan to give Italy much of Abyssinia; its leak caused public outrage and it was dropped.
Trade restrictions imposed on Italy by the League in 1935; they excluded oil, coal and steel and were lifted in 1936.
Understanding between Mussolini and Hitler announced in late 1936, marking Italy's shift towards Germany.
May 1939 military alliance between Italy and Germany committing each to support the other in war.
Italy's status from September 1939 to June 1940: aligned with Germany but not yet fighting, because it was unprepared.
Emperor of Ethiopia (Abyssinia), who appealed in person to the League in June 1936 after Italy's conquest.

questions.prompt: Which motive is LEAST convincing as a reason for Mussolini's invasion of Abyssinia?
options: Avenging the Italian defeat at Adwa in 1896
Prestige and a 'new Roman Empire'
Securing large oil reserves in Abyssinia
Distracting from economic problems at home
questions.explanation: Abyssinia had no significant known oil. Revenge for Adwa, prestige, settlement land and domestic propaganda were the main motives.

questions.text: In April 1935 Britain, France and Italy formed the ___ Front against German rearmament.
questions.explanation: The front collapsed within months over Abyssinia and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935.

questions.statement: League sanctions against Italy in 1935 included a ban on oil exports to Italy.
questions.explanation: Oil was excluded, partly because the USA (not a member) would keep supplying it and partly because Britain and France feared driving Italy towards Hitler.

questions.prompt: Why was the Hoare–Laval Pact so damaging to the League?
options: It showed Britain and France were willing to reward aggression behind the League's back
It brought the USA into the League
It led to Italy's immediate defeat
It expelled Germany from the League
questions.explanation: The leaked plan offered Italy about two-thirds of Abyssinia. Hoare resigned, but the League's credibility was shattered.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
questions.explanation: December 1934, April 1935, October 1935, December 1935, May 1936.

questions.prompt: Which British decision kept the Suez Canal open to Italian ships during the war?
options: Fear that closing it might provoke war with Italy
A treaty giving Italy ownership of the canal
Pressure from the USA
A League vote to keep it open
questions.explanation: Closing the canal would have crippled Italy's supply lines, but Britain judged the risk of war too high.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its description.

pairs.right: Ethiopian victory over an earlier Italian invasion
Border clash used as a pretext
Where Haile Selassie addressed the League

questions.explanation: Italy also used poison gas against Ethiopian troops and civilians during the campaign.

questions.text: Emperor ___ warned the League in 1936 that 'it is us today, it will be you tomorrow'.
questions.explanation: His appeal failed; sanctions were lifted in July 1936.

questions.statement: Italy used chemical weapons in Abyssinia.
questions.explanation: Italian forces used mustard gas, in breach of the 1925 Geneva Protocol, which Italy had signed.

questions.prompt: What was the most important international consequence of the Abyssinian crisis?
options: Italy and Germany drew closer and collective security was discredited
Britain and Italy formed a lasting alliance
The League gained new authority
The USA joined the League
questions.explanation: Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936 while attention was on Abyssinia, and Italy moved towards the Axis.

questions.text: Mussolini first spoke of a Rome–Berlin ___ in November 1936.
questions.explanation: He described Europe turning around an 'axis' between Rome and Berlin.

questions.prompt: How did Italy intervene in the Spanish Civil War?
options: It sent tens of thousands of troops and aircraft to help Franco
It supported the Republic
It stayed strictly neutral
It sent only food aid
questions.explanation: Italy's Corpo Truppe Volontarie fought for the Nationalists, at great cost to Italy's economy and military stocks.

questions.statement: In 1934 Mussolini moved troops to the Brenner Pass to deter a Nazi takeover of Austria.
questions.explanation: After the murder of Chancellor Dollfuss in July 1934, Mussolini acted to protect Austria; by 1938 he accepted the Anschluss.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
items: Italy declares war on Britain and France
questions.explanation: November 1936, November 1937, April 1939, May 1939, June 1940.

questions.prompt: Why did Italy declare 'non-belligerence' in September 1939?
options: Mussolini opposed Hitler's war on principle
Italy's armed forces and economy were not ready for a major war
Britain had paid Italy to stay neutral
The Pact of Steel forbade Italy to fight
questions.explanation: Mussolini had told Hitler Italy would not be ready until about 1942–43; Abyssinia and Spain had drained resources.

questions.prompt: When did Italy finally enter the Second World War?
options: September 1939
June 1940, as France was collapsing
December 1941
June 1941
questions.explanation: Mussolini declared war on 10 June 1940, hoping to share the spoils of a German victory.

questions.prompt: Match each agreement to its content.

pairs.right: Britain tried to keep Italy from Germany
Mussolini posed as peacemaker over Czechoslovakia

questions.explanation: Britain kept trying to separate Italy from Germany until 1939.

questions.text: Italy invaded ___ in April 1939, partly to match German gains.
questions.explanation: Albania was already an Italian client state; the invasion followed Germany's occupation of Prague in March 1939.

questions.statement: Italy left the League of Nations in 1937.
questions.explanation: Italy announced its withdrawal in December 1937, following Japan (1933) and Germany (1933).

questions.prompt: Which historian is best known for portraying Mussolini's foreign policy as opportunistic showmanship rather than a coherent plan?
options: Denis Mack Smith
A.J.P. Taylor
Fritz Fischer
John Lewis Gaddis
questions.explanation: Mack Smith stressed propaganda and improvisation; others, such as MacGregor Knox, argue Mussolini pursued consistent expansionist goals.
